title: Training Webpage Template: User Guide
text:
Welcome to the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template User Guide!

What is the template?
The SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template helps you create a consistent, reusable and FAIR website for your training. No programming is needed: you fill in text files and write your materials in Markdown, and the website is built and published for you.


How is a training website organised?

A landing page introduces the training as a whole, and links to every training instance.
A training instance is one time the training is given, or one version of its materials, with its own schedule, team and materials.



Which trainings is it for?
Most kinds: online or in-person, recurring courses and workshops, one-off trainings, self-paced training, and training in cohorts. See Training instances for how each one fits.


What does this guide cover?
Everything from an empty template to a published, citable training website: setting up your copy, the landing page, your training instances and materials, and making your training FAIR.
No experience with Git, Python or Quarto is needed!

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.1 Install the software
This chapter takes you through everything you need to do once, at the start, to get your own training website. You will create your own copy of the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template, publish it as a website, and set it up on your computer so you can edit it.
Once you are done, the next chapter, Regular workflow, shows the few steps you repeat every time you update your website.
To work with the template, you need a free GitHub account and four free programs. If you already have some of them, you can skip those.
Install each program with the default settings. Then open Visual Studio Code (VS Code) once, to check that it starts.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.2 Create your repository
A repository is the folder on GitHub that holds everything for your training: the information about it, the materials, and the website. You will create your own repository as a copy of the template. The template itself stays unchanged.

Open the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template on GitHub.
In the top-right corner of the page, click the green Use this template button and select Create a new repository.



Fill in the form:

Turn Include all branches on. This is required: the template keeps the landing page and each training instance in separate branches (see Repository structure), and you need all of them.
Under Owner, select the GitHub organisation or account where the repository should live, for example SciLifeLab-Training, NBISweden, or your personal account.
Under Repository name, enter a short name in lowercase, with hyphens instead of spaces, for example introduction-to-r. The name becomes part of your website address, so choose it carefully.
Under Visibility, choose Public, so participants can see the website and materials.

Click Create repository.


GitHub now opens your new repository. Check the name at the top of the page: it should be the name you just chose, not the template’s name.







TipWorking with others? Add collaborators (optional)





If other people will help develop or maintain the training, give them access to the repository. You can also do this later.

In your repository, click Settings. 
Under Access in the menu on the left, click Collaborators and teams. 
Click Add people or Add teams.
Search for the person or team, choose a role, and click Add. 

The options you see depend on whether the repository belongs to you or to an organisation, and on your permissions in that organisation.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.3 Publish your website
Your new repository already contains a ready-made copy of the template website, and GitHub usually publishes it and sets it up by itself. In this step you check two settings, and add your website link to your repository’s main page.

Check that your website is online

In your repository, click Settings, then Pages in the menu on the left. 
At the top of the page, look for Your site is live at, followed by your website address. It looks like https://ORGANISATION.github.io/REPOSITORY-NAME/, with your organisation (or user name) and repository name filled in. 

For now, your website shows the template’s example content. It changes to your own content the first time you upload a change.






NoteDon’t see “Your site is live at”?





Sometimes GitHub doesn’t switch on publishing by itself. You can do it yourself:

On the same page, under Source, choose Deploy from a branch.
Under Branch, choose gh-pages and / (root), and click Save. 
Wait a minute or two and refresh the page. Your site is live at now appears at the top.






Check that your website can be updated
Every time you upload a change, GitHub runs a small automatic process that rebuilds your website. This process needs permission to update the website.

Click Settings, then Actions → General in the menu on the left.
Scroll down to Workflow permissions, and check that Read and write permissions is selected. 







NoteIs “Read repository contents and packages permissions” selected instead?





Select Read and write permissions and click Save.
If you can’t select it because the option is greyed out, your organisation controls this setting. Ask an administrator of the organisation to allow it for your repository.





Add the website link to your repository
Show the website address on your repository’s main page, so you can always find your website quickly:

Click the Code tab to go back to the repository’s main page. 
On the right-hand side, next to About, click the gear icon ⚙️.
Tick Use your GitHub Pages website and click Save changes.

title: 2  Set up your training
section: 2.4 Open the repository on your computer
text:
2.4 Open the repository on your computer
So far, your repository only exists on GitHub. To edit it, you make a copy on your computer. This is called cloning.
Working on a copy has a big advantage: nothing you change is visible to anyone else until you decide to upload it. You can try things out, look at the result, and undo mistakes, all safely on your own computer.

On your repository’s main page on GitHub, click the green Code button, make sure HTTPS is selected, and copy the address.

Open VS Code and click Clone Git Repository on the start screen. If you don’t see it, open View → Command Palette, type Git: Clone and press Enter.

Paste the HTTPS address you copied and press Enter.
Choose where to save the repository on your computer, for example a folder called GitHub inside Documents, and click Select as Repository Destination. 
When VS Code asks whether to open the repository, click Open.

The files and folders of your repository now appear in the Explorer panel on the left side of VS Code. Throughout this guide, you open files by clicking them there.
If VS Code suggests installing recommended extensions, click Install. They help VS Code understand the files used in the template.







TipPrefer the terminal?





cd ~/Documents/GitHub
git clone https://github.com/ORGANISATION/REPOSITORY-NAME.git
Then open the new folder in VS Code with File → Open Folder…

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.5 Set up the environment
Your website is built by a few small Python scripts that come with the template. These scripts need one extra Python package. In this step you install it in a separate, self-contained environment inside your repository folder, so it doesn’t interfere with anything else on your computer.
You only do this once for each repository. You don’t need to understand the commands: copy each one exactly as shown.

Open a terminal
A terminal is a window where you type commands. In VS Code, choose Terminal → New Terminal.

The terminal opens at the bottom of the window, already inside your repository folder.
To run a command from this guide, copy it, paste it into the terminal, and press Enter.



Check the software
First, check that Git, Python and Quarto were installed correctly. Run these commands one by one:

macOS and LinuxWindows


git --version
python3 --version
quarto --version


git --version
python --version
quarto --version



Each command should print a version number, for example Python 3.12.4 (see image above). If one says command not found, install that program again, restart VS Code, and try again.


Create the environment
Run these three commands one by one. The last one can take a minute.

macOS and LinuxWindows


python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt


python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt



The first command creates the environment, the second switches it on, and the third installs what the scripts need. When the environment is switched on, the terminal line starts with (.venv):
(.venv) username@computer introduction-to-r %



Let VS Code switch on the environment
The environment has to be switched on each time you open a new terminal. You can let VS Code do that for you:

Press Cmd+Shift+P (macOS) or Ctrl+Shift+P (Windows and Linux).
Type Python: Select Interpreter and press Enter.
Choose the option that shows .venv.


From now on, every new terminal you open in this repository starts with the environment switched on.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
You’re all set!
Your training has its own repository and website, and your computer is ready to edit it. You won’t need to repeat any of these steps for this training.
Continue with Regular workflow to make your first change and see it appear on your website.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.1 Open your training
This chapter shows the steps you repeat every time you work on your training website: open your training, preview it, make your changes, and publish them.
The steps are always the same, whether you change a date, add a team member or write a new page of materials. The cheat sheet at the end of this chapter lists all of them in one table.
Each time you start working, open your repository in VS Code and make sure you have the latest version.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
Open VS Code. It usually reopens the repository you worked on last. 
If not, choose File → Open Recent, or File → Open Folder… and select your repository folder.

Get the latest version. If you work together with others, they may have uploaded changes since you last worked. In the bottom-left corner of VS Code, click the circular arrows next to the branch name (Synchronize Changes). This downloads their changes to your computer.



Which part of your website are you working on?
The bottom-left corner of VS Code also shows the branch you are working on. Your repository keeps each part of your training website in its own branch (see Repository structure):

main: the training landing page.
release- followed by four digits, for example release-2605: one training instance in May 2026. In your template copy, it will say release-0000


Before you start editing, check that you are on the branch you want to change. For your first change below, stay on main.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.2 Preview your website
A preview shows your website in your web browser while you work on it, before anything is published. The preview runs on your own computer, so only you can see it. This lets you check every change before your collaborators or participants see it.
To start the preview, open a terminal (Terminal → New Terminal, see Open a terminal) and run:
python scripts/preview.py

Quarto now builds your website. After a few seconds, it opens in your web browser.

If it doesn’t open by itself, copy the address shown in the terminal, for example http://localhost:4268/, and paste it into your browser.
Keep the preview running while you work. Each time you save a file (Cmd+S (macOS) or Ctrl+S (Windows and Linux)), the preview updates by itself.

To run other commands while the preview is running, open a second terminal with Terminal → New Terminal. The terminal running the preview is busy.
To stop the preview when you are done, click in the terminal where it runs and press Ctrl+C.







TipAnother way to start the preview: the Preview button





When a page file (ending in .qmd) is open in VS Code, you can also click the Preview button in the top-right corner of the editor.

The website then opens inside VS Code. To see it in your browser instead, click Open in Browser.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.3 Make a change
Almost everything on your website comes from the files in the data folder: the title, dates, team, schedule, and so on. You change your website by changing these files, without touching any code.
How these files are organised is explained in Repository structure. For now, we focus on making one change and publishing it, so you can practice the whole process from start to finish.
As a first change, try changing the title of your training:

In the Explorer panel, open the data folder and click course.yml.



Scroll down a bit and find the line:
title: "Training title"
Change the text between the quotation marks to your training’s title, for example:
title: "Introduction to R"



Save the file with Cmd+S (macOS) or Ctrl+S (Windows and Linux).

The new title now appears at the top of the website preview in your browser.







Important



The data files are very sensitive to layout! Keep the quotation marks, and keep the indentation at the start of each line exactly as it is. If the preview shows an error after you save, check the file layout first. The lines starting with # are explanations: they don’t appear on the website.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.4 Commit and push your changes
Your change is now saved on your computer, but nobody else can see it yet. Publishing it takes two steps, both in VS Code’s Source Control panel:

Commit: save a version of your changes, with a short description of what you changed. Each commit is kept, so you can always see what changed and when.
Push: upload your commits to GitHub. GitHub then updates your website automatically.


Click the Source Control icon on the left side of VS Code. Your changed files are listed under Changes.
You changed only course.yml, but you probably see more files, for example files in the _generated folder. That’s expected: the template updates these files automatically from your data files, while the preview runs. Depending on what you change, you may also see README.md, CITATION.cff or .zenodo.json. Always commit all changed files together.

Hover over the word Changes and click the + next to it (Stage All Changes). This tells VS Code to include all changed files in your commit. They move to Staged Changes.

In the Message box at the top, describe your change, for example Change the training title.

Click Commit.
Click Sync Changes to push your commit to GitHub.








Note



The first time you push, VS Code may ask you to sign in to GitHub. Follow the instructions in your browser, then return to VS Code.








Important



If you want to make changes on several branches, commit and push your changes on one branch before you switch to another branch. Changes you haven’t committed yet move along with you to the other branch, where you might commit them by mistake.








TipChanged something by mistake?





Before you commit, you can undo all changes to a file: in the Source Control panel, hover over the file and click the curved arrow (Discard Changes). The file goes back to how it was at your last commit.

You only need to do this for the files you changed yourself, such as data/course.yml. The files the template updates automatically, for example in the _generated folder, go back by themselves: as soon as you discard your own change, the preview rebuilds them, and they disappear from the list after a few seconds.
This only works while the preview is running. If they are still listed, start the preview (python scripts/preview.py) and wait a few seconds.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.5 Check the published website
After you push your local changes to GitHub to be published, GitHub rebuilds your website by itself. This usually takes one or two minutes. You can follow it on GitHub:

Open your repository on GitHub and click the Actions tab.

Wait until both of these show a green checkmark:

deploy-landing (or deploy-instance, when you changed a training instance): builds your website;
pages build and deployment: publishes it.


A yellow dot means it is still running.
Open your website with the link under About on your repository’s main page, see About link.







Tip



Still seeing the old version? Wait a minute and refresh the page. Browsers sometimes show an older copy for a short while.
A red cross in the Actions tab means something went wrong. Click it to see the error message, or see the cheat sheet below.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
4.1 Branches
You now know the routine for making a change to your training website, and how to publish it (see Regular workflow).
Before fully making the template your own, with the information and materials of your training, it helps to know how the repository is organised. This chapter shows you where different parts of the website live, so you always know where to make a change.
Your training repository is divided into branches. Each branch holds the files for one part of your website. A new repository made from the template has three branches: main, release-0000 and gh-pages.
Each of these branches holds the files for one part of your website:
Because each training instance has its own branch, you can prepare the next training without changing the website of an earlier one. Participants of earlier trainings can always go back to the materials as they were.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
The main branch holds the landing page: the general page about your training, with its description, learning outcomes and team, and links to every time the training is given.

The gh-pages branch holds the published website: the finished pages that visitors see. GitHub builds them from your other branches and updates this branch automatically every time you push a change.







Important



Never edit the gh-pages branch yourself. GitHub updates it automatically every time you push a change to one of the other branches.



The release-0000 branch is an example training instance: the website for one time the training is given, with its dates, schedule, practical information, team and training materials. You use it as the starting point for each new training instance, which gets a branch of its own.




Branch names
A training instance branch is named release- followed by the year and month of the training, written as YYMM. For example, release-2705 is the training instance held in May 2027.


An example
This is what the branches look like in a repository for a training that has been given twice, in May 2026 and May 2027:
Your repository
│
├── main              The landing page: the general page about your
│                     training, with links to every training instance.
│
├── release-2605      The website of your training in May 2026.
├── release-2705      The website of your training in May 2027.
│
│
└── gh-pages          The published website. Updated automatically.
In this repository, you would work on these branches:



I want to…
I work on branch…




Change the landing page
main


Edit the materials of the May 2026 training
release-2605


Fix a typo on the May 2027 website
release-2705


Set up the next training instance
A new release- branch: see Training instances









Note



You work on one branch at a time. To learn how to switch to another branch in VS Code, see Switch branch.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
4.2 Three kinds of files
When you open a branch of your repository in VS Code, you see many files and folders. Most of these you never have to edit, you only have to work with a few of them. On all branches, the files fall into three groups:








Icon
Kind
What it means for you




✏️
Files you edit
Your information and materials. This is where you make your changes.


🔄
Files that are updated automatically
The template creates and updates these files automatically. You should not edit them, but if you accidentally do, your edits will automatically be overwritten.


🔒
Files you can leave alone
The parts that make the template work, you never need to change these.









Tip



The automatically updated files 🔄 often appear in the Source Control panel when you only edited one ✏️ file. That’s expected: commit them together with your own changes, as described in Commit and push your changes.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
4.3 Files on the main branch
On the main branch, everything for your training’s landing page lives in these files and folders:

The table below explains what each one is for, and whether you edit it ✏️, it’s updated automatically 🔄, or you can leave it alone 🔒.








File or folder
What it contains
Kind of file




data/course.yml
The title, description, learning outcomes, etc. of your training, and how others may reuse and cite it
✏️


data/team.yml
The people behind the training
✏️


data/website.yml
The logos, button texts and footer of the landing page
✏️


data/instances.yml
The list of training instances, with links to their websites
✏️


img/
The images and logos used on the landing page
✏️


docs/
The README for your training (_template-README.md), which you copy over README.md when you start, and documentation for developers of the template
✏️


README.md
The description shown on your repository’s main page on GitHub. The parts between <!-- generated:... --> lines are updated automatically; you can edit the rest
✏️ 🔄


_generated/
The sections of the landing page, built from your data files
🔄


CITATION.cff
How to cite your training, built from your data files
🔄


.zenodo.json
The information Zenodo uses when you publish your training, built from your data files
🔄


LICENSE.md
The full text of the licence of your training: CC BY 4.0, unless you choose another licence in data/course.yml. Only replace it if you do
✏️🔒


CONTRIBUTING.md
How others can report problems and suggest improvements to your training.Ready to use, but you can adapt it if you like
✏️🔒


index.qmd, _sections/
The building blocks that put the landing page together
🔒


styles.css
The look of the website: colours, fonts and layout
🔒


_template/
Information about the template itself, used only while template mode is on. You can delete it once you’ve switched template mode off
🔒


scripts/, tests/
The scripts that build the website, and the checks that test them
🔒


.github/
The automatic processes that publish your website on GitHub
🔒


.vscode/
Settings for VS Code, such as the extensions it recommends when you open the repository
🔒


.gitignore
The list of files that stay on your computer and are never uploaded to GitHub, such as your preview and environment
🔒


_quarto.yml, requirements.txt, requirements-dev.txt
Settings for Quarto, and the Python packages the scripts need
🔒



When you preview your website, a few more folders appear on your computer: _site/ (the website itself), .quarto/ and .venv/ (your environment). They are listed in .gitignore, so they are never uploaded to GitHub, and you can ignore them.

title: 4  Repository structure
section: 4.4 Files on a training instance branch
text:
4.4 Files on a training instance branch
A training instance branch has the same structure as main, plus the information pages of that training instance, your training materials, and notes for instructors who teach or reuse the training.

The table below explains what each one is for, and whether you edit it ✏️, it’s updated automatically 🔄, or you can leave it alone 🔒.








File or folder
What it contains
Kind of file




data/course.yml
The title, dates, location and description of this training instance, and how others may reuse and cite it (required)
✏️


data/team.yml
The organisers, instructors and helpers (required)
✏️


data/website.yml
The logos, texts and sections of the overview page, and the footer (required)
✏️


data/schedule.yml
The schedule of the training (optional)
✏️


data/announcements.yml, practicalities.yml, preparation.yml, faq.yml, resources.yml
The information pages (all optional)
✏️


content/
Your training materials
✏️


instructors/
Notes for instructors: timing, preparation and teaching notes for each module. Not shown on the website, but anyone can read it on GitHub
✏️


img/
The images, logos and photos used on the website
✏️


docs/
The README for your training (_template-README.md), which you copy over README.md when you start, example files used in the example module pages; and documentation for developers of the template
✏️


README.md
The description GitHub shows when someone opens this branch. The parts between <!-- generated:... --> lines are updated automatically; you can edit the rest
✏️ 🔄


CONTRIBUTING.md
How others can report problems and suggest improvements to your training. Ready to use, but you can adapt it if you like
✏️🔒


LICENSE.md
The full text of the licence of your training: CC BY 4.0, unless you choose another licence in data/course.yml. Only replace it if you do
✏️🔒


_generated/
The sections of the website, built from your data files when you preview. Not uploaded to GitHub
🔄


CITATION.cff, .zenodo.json
How to cite this training instance, and the information Zenodo uses, built from your data files
🔄


index.qmd, schedule.qmd, team.qmd and the other .qmd files
The pages of the website. They collect their content from your data files
🔒


_sections/, js/, styles.css
The building blocks, interactive parts and look of the website
🔒


scripts/, .github/
The scripts that build the website, and the automatic processes that publish it
🔒


_quarto.yml, requirements.txt, .gitignore
Settings for Quarto, the Python packages the scripts need, and the list of files that are never uploaded to GitHub
🔒



When you preview your website, a few more folders appear on your computer: _site/ (the website itself), .quarto/ and .venv/ (your environment). They are listed in .gitignore, so they are never uploaded to GitHub, and you can ignore them.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
4.5 Data files
As the tables above show, most of the files you edit in the main branch as well as the instance branches are data files: the files ending in .yml in the data folder.
When you open a data file, for example data/course.yml on the main branch, you see three kinds of text. VS Code shows each in its own colour:


Explanations (grey in the screenshot): lines that start with #. They explain how the file works and what each field does, and don’t appear on your website. You can delete them if you prefer a shorter file, but they are useful to keep while you are getting to know the template.
Field names (green): the word before the colon, for example title:. They tell the template where each piece of information goes on your website. Never change field names. If you do, the template can’t find that information any more.
Values (blue): the text after the colon, usually between quotation marks. This is what you change. It is the information that appears on your website.

For example, in this line:
title: "Training title"
title is the field name: leave it as it is. "Training title" is the value: replace it with the title of your training.






Note



The colours depend on the colour theme you use in VS Code, so yours may look different from the screenshot. The rule is always the same: lines starting with # are explanations, the word before the colon is the field name, and the text after the colon is the value you change.








Important



Data files are very sensitive to layout:

Keep the spaces at the start of each line exactly as they are. They show which information belongs together.
Keep the quotation marks around values.
Lines starting with - are list items. To add an item, copy a whole line and change its value.

If the preview shows an error after you save a data file, check these first. The error message usually names the file and the line.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
Before you start
The landing page is the front door of your training. It introduces the training as a whole, and helps visitors decide whether to register, or which training instance to open.
The figure below shows the parts of the landing page, and the names this guide uses for them.
In this chapter, you will learn how to:
How to create a training instance and add it to the landing page is explained in the next chapter, Training instances.
Everything in this chapter happens on the main branch, and almost all of it in three data files in the data folder:
Not sure how a data file works? See Data files.
Work as described in Regular workflow:
The cheat sheet at the end of this chapter sums up which file to open and what to change for each part of the landing page.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.1 Switch off template mode
Your repository starts as a copy of the template, so it still presents itself as the template, in two places:

the README.md file, the description shown on your repository’s main page on GitHub, which still describes the template instead of your training;
the yellow Want to use this template? banner at the top of the landing page (see the overview image above).

In this section, you replace the README and then switch off template mode, so your repository presents your own training.

Replace the README
The template comes with a ready-made README for your training, in docs/_template-README.md. Copy it over the current README, which describes the template:

In the Explorer panel, open the docs folder and then _template-README.md.

Select all text (Cmd+A or Ctrl+A) and copy it.
Open README.md in the main folder of your repository, select all text, and paste, so the copied text replaces it.

Delete the note at the top of the file, between <!-- and -->, and the line starting with > **Template:**.
Fill in the parts marked Write this yourself. The other parts, between <!-- generated:... --> lines, are filled in automatically from your data files.
Save the file.




Remove the template banner

Open data/website.yml.
Find the line:
template: true
Change it to:
template: false

Save the file with Cmd+S (macOS) or Ctrl+S (Windows and Linux).

This changes three things:

The yellow banner disappears from the landing page.
The generated parts of your new README now show your training’s details, from your data files.
CITATION.cff and .zenodo.json now describe your training instead of the template.








NoteOptional: delete the template files you no longer need





Two things on main are only needed while you set up your repository:

The docs/_template-README.md file (keep the rest of the docs folder)
The _template folder

You can delete both: in the Explorer panel, right-click each and choose Delete.
If you ever set template: true again, the preview stops with an error, because the _template folder is missing.









Tip



The README shows the details you have filled in so far. Did you not fill in the data files yet? No problem: the README updates by itself every time you change them.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.2 Customise the look
You can make the landing page your own by changing the organisation logos, the button texts and the banner image. All of these are in data/website.yml. Open it, and work through the parts below.

Logos
The logos in the hero show the organisations behind your training. The SciLifeLab logo is always shown on the right. Your other logos appear to its left.
Add a logo

Save your logo as an SVG or PNG file.






Tip



Use a white version of your logo, or one made for a dark background, so it stands out against the dark hero.


Copy the file into the img/logos folder: drag it from your computer onto the folder in the Explorer panel in VS Code.
In data/website.yml, find the hero part:
hero:
  logos:
    - src: "img/logos/SciLifeLab_Logotype_NEG.png"
      alt: "SciLifeLab"
      height: 56
      primary: true
Add your logo below the existing one, with these lines:

src: where the file is: img/logos/ followed by the file name;
alt: the name of the organisation;
height (optional): the height of the logo in pixels, 56 if you leave it out.

For example:

IMAGE

Save the file, and check the preview. If the logos look like different sizes, adjust their height until they look about the same.

The logo with primary: true (SciLifeLab) is always shown on the right. Your other logos appear to its left, in the same order as in the list.
Remove a logo

In data/website.yml, delete all lines of the logo you want to remove, from - src: to its last line.
Save the file.
Optional: if you no longer need the logo file, delete it from the img/logos folder. In VS Code, right-click the file and choose Delete.



Button texts
You can change the text on the two hero buttons, and the heading of the All training instances banner:

In data/website.yml, find the labels part:
labels:
  hero_view_current_label: "Take me to the current instance"
  hero_registration_open_label: "Register now"
  instances_band_title: "All training instances"
Change the text between the quotation marks. For example:
hero_view_current_label: "Go to the latest training"
hero_registration_open_label: "Sign up"
Save the file.

This only changes the texts. Where the buttons lead, and when they are shown, is set in data/instances.yml: see Training instances.


Banner image
The All training instances banner shows a decorative image next to the buttons. You can replace it with an image that fits your training.

Copy your image into the img/images folder: drag it from your computer onto the folder in the Explorer panel in VS Code.






Tip



Use a landscape image. The image is cropped automatically to fill the space, so keep the important part near the middle.


In data/website.yml, find:
instances_band:
  image: "img/images/navet-band.png"
Replace navet-band.png with the file name of your image, for example:
instances_band:
  image: "img/images/my-training-banner.jpg"
Save the file, and check the preview at different widths of your browser window.

To show no image at all, change it to image: "".






TipIs the important part of your image cut off?





You can choose which part of the image stays visible. This is the only change in this guide in styles.css, the file that controls the look of the website, so make it carefully:

Open styles.css and search for .instances-band__image (Cmd+F or Ctrl+F).
In that block, find:
object-position: center;
Change center to the part you want to keep. For example, center top keeps the top of the image, and 30% center moves the visible part to the left.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.3 Describe your training
What the landing page says about your training comes from two data files: data/course.yml describes the training, and data/team.yml the people behind it. The information you enter in these files is also used in the README and the citation of your training, and helps people find it in Zenodo and training registries such as TeSS.
Both files contain explanations at the top and between the fields, in the lines starting with #. This section covers the main points; the explanations in the files give the details.

How to fill in a data file
You only change the values: the text after the colon. See Data files for how a data file is built. Values come in three forms:
A single line of text, between quotation marks:
title: "Introduction to R"
Several paragraphs, after |. Start each line with the same number of spaces, and separate paragraphs with an empty line:
description: |
  This training introduces R, a free and widely used programming
  language for data analysis.

  Through short demonstrations and hands-on exercises, you learn how to
  read, clean, summarise and plot your data.
A list: each line starting with - is one item. To add an item, copy a whole line, paste it below, and change the text. To remove an item, delete its whole line:
keywords:
  - "R"
  - "Data analysis"
  - "Data visualisation"


The training: course.yml
Open data/course.yml and work through it from top to bottom:








Field
Where it appears
What to fill in




title
The hero, and the browser tab
The name of your training


subtitle
The hero, below the title
One sentence about the training (optional)


description
The Training content card
What the training covers, in a few paragraphs


learning_outcomes
The Learning outcomes card
What participants can do after the training


keywords
The Keywords card
Four or five short terms that describe the subject


topics
The Topics covered card
The main topics, as short phrases


language, target_audience, expertise_level, organizers, funding
Not on the landing page: in the README, the citation and the information for training registries
See the explanations in the file


licence, licence_url (under reuse)
The footer (“Licensed under …”), the README and the citation
CC BY 4.0 by default.



The other fields under reuse can stay empty for now:

doi, release_date and zenodo_communities belong to publishing your training on Zenodo, and are explained in FAIRification.
licence_id, website_url and preferred_citation can stay empty for most trainings. The template works out the address of your website, and creates the citation from your team, title and DOI.

Example of a filled-in course.yml:
IMAGE






Tip




Subtitle: keep it to one sentence, and start it with an action verb such as Learn, Understand, Explore, Build or Apply.
Learning outcomes describe what participants will be able to do after the training. For guidance, see the SciLifeLab Training Hub resources on writing learning outcomes.
Optional fields: to leave out the subtitle, use subtitle: "". To leave out the funding, keep funding: [].
Licence: if you change it, also replace the text in LICENSE.md in the main folder of your repository with the full text of your new licence.





The team: team.yml
The Founders and Contributors cards at the bottom of the landing page list the people in data/team.yml. They are also credited in the README and the citation of your training.
Open data/team.yml and fill in each person. The comments at the top of the file explain every field. To add a person, copy a whole entry, from - given_names: to the line before the next person, paste it below, and change the values. To remove a person, delete their whole entry.
Example of a filled-in team.yml:
IMAGE






Important



Every person needs given_names, family_names, roles (Founder or Contributor) and affiliation. If one is missing, the preview shows an error that names the person and the missing field.

title: 6  Training instances
text:
Before you start
A training instance is one time your training is given, for example in May 2027. Each training instance has its own branch in your repository, and from that its own website is created with dates, schedule, team and materials.
The landing page can link to all instances:
In this chapter, you will learn how to:
How to switch off template mode and fill in the website of a training instance (its dates, schedule, team and materials) is explained in the next chapters, Instance pages - Data files and Instance pages - Content.
In this chapter, you work on two branches: the new release- branch, and main for the landing page.

title: 6  Training instances
section: 6.1 Create your first new training instance
text:
6.1 Create your first new training instance

Choose a name
Each training instance branch is named release- followed by the year and month in which the training instance is given, written as YYMM (see Branches). For example:







Training instance
Branch name




May 2027
release-2705


November 2027
release-2711



The four digits also become the address of its website: https://ORGANISATION.github.io/REPOSITORY-NAME/2705/.






NoteSelf-paced training: what is a training instance?





In self-paced training, participants start whenever they like, so there is no “time the training is given”. Instead, think of a training instance as a version of your materials:

Name the branch after the year and month the version is released. For example, release-2705 for a version published in May 2027.
Create a new training instance when you update the materials substantially, for example a new module or a revised structure. Small fixes, such as typos, go into the current training instance.
Earlier versions stay online. Participants who started with an earlier version can finish with the materials they began with.

Some settings will work differently for self-paced training.

On the main branch in data/instances.yml: the latest version is the current training instance. If participants don’t register, set registration_url: "".
On the instance branches: this will be explained further in Instance pages - Data files and Instance pages - Content.










NoteTraining in cohorts: one training instance per cohort?





If your training runs in cohorts, groups of participants who follow the same training at different times, how you set up your training instances depends on how your training is organised: does each cohort need its own website, or do the cohorts share one?
Option 1: one training instance per cohort

When: each cohort has its own dates, schedule, team or announcements.
Branch name: the year and month the cohort starts, for example release-2702 for a cohort starting in February 2027, and release-2709 for the next one in September.
What it represents: one cohort, with its own website. Each new cohort starts from the previous one, as described in Create additional training instances.

Option 2: one training instance for several cohorts

When: the cohorts follow the same materials and website, and only their start dates differ.
Branch name: the year and month the materials are released, as for self-paced training, for example release-2702.
What it represents: a version of your materials. List the cohorts and their dates on the website, for example in the announcements or practicalities (see Instance pages - Data files). Create a new training instance only when the materials change substantially.

Each branch name must be unique, so with option 1, two cohorts can’t start in the same month.
This is the advice of the SciLifeLab Training Hub, but you know your training best: choose the setup that suits it.





Switch branch
You create a new branch as a copy of an existing one, so first switch to the branch you want to copy.
For your first training instance: switch to release-0000, the example training instance that comes with the template.
To switch branch in VS Code:

Click the branch name in the bottom-left corner of VS Code.
In the list that opens at the top, choose the branch, for example release-0000. Branches that are only on GitHub so far start with origin/: choose those to get them on your computer.

Screenshot: the branch list in VS Code, with release-0000 selected.
The files in the Explorer panel change to the files of that branch, and the bottom-left corner shows its name.


Create the branch

Check that the bottom-left corner shows the branch you want to copy.
Click the branch name, and choose Create new branch… in the list that opens at the top.
Type the name of the new branch, for example release-2705, and press Enter.
Open the Source Control panel and click Publish Branch. This puts the new branch on GitHub.

Screenshot: Create new branch in the branch list, and the Publish Branch button.
As soon as the branch is on GitHub, GitHub builds its website, as with every push: see Check the published website.

title: 6  Training instances
section: 6.2 Add an instance to the landing page
text:
6.2 Add an instance to the landing page
Creating a release- branch does not add it to the landing page automatically. You add it yourself, in data/instances.yml on the main branch.

Make sure you’ve committed any changes you made on your new branch, and switch to the main branch, as described in Switch branch.
Open data/instances.yml. It lists the training instances the landing page links to: one entry per training instance, from - slug: to sort_key:. The guiding comments at the top of the file explain each field.
The template list contains example training instances. Change the first one, with slug: "0000", into your own training instance: change its slug, label, instance_url and sort_key. Add a url to a registration page or form under registration_url if registration is open.
For example, for a May 2027 instance:
   - slug: "2705"
      label: "May 2027"
      status: current
      visible: true
      show_in_hero: true
      instance_url: "./2705/"
      registration_url: ""
      sort_key: 202705
Delete the other examples, 2505 and 2411: each whole entry, from - slug: to sort_key:. They are part of the template for demonstration purposes and link to websites that don’t exist in your repository.
Save the file, and check the preview. Then commit and push your changes.

If you break one of the rules described in the file, the preview shows an error that explains what to fix.






TipOptional: delete release-0000





Once your own training instance exists, you no longer need the example on release-0000. You can keep it, to look up how something was set up in the template, or delete it:

Delete the branch: on your repository’s main page on GitHub, click Branches, then the bin icon next to release-0000.
Delete its website: on the gh-pages branch on GitHub, open the 0000 folder, click ⋯ at the top right, and choose Delete directory.

Only delete it when your own first training instance is ready. Your later training instances start from your own previous one, so you don’t need release-0000 for those. But once deleted, it’s gone!

title: 6  Training instances
text:
6.3 Create additional training instances
The next time your training is given, start from your previous training instance rather than from release-0000. That way, everything you prepared last time comes along: your materials, instructor notes, team and settings. The previous training instance keeps its own branch and website, so participants can always go back to the materials as they were.

Switch to your previous training instance, for example release-2705, and create a new branch from it, for example release-2711, as described in Create your first new training instance.
Update the information of the new training instance, such as its dates, schedule and team: see Instance pages - Data files.
Switch to main, and open data/instances.yml.
Add the new training instance: copy the entry of the current one, paste it at the top of the list, and change slug, label, instance_url and sort_key.
Make the new training instance the current one. In the entry of the previous training instance, change status: current to status: previous, and show_in_hero: true to show_in_hero: false.
Save the file, check the preview, and commit and push.

IMAGE






Important



If your previous training instance was published on Zenodo, empty version_doi and release_date under reuse in data/course.yml of the new branch: they belong to the previous training instance. See FAIRification.

title: 7  Instance pages - Data files
text:
Before you start
Each training instance has its own website: an overview page, a schedule, the training materials, and information pages such as the syllabus and the team. In this chapter, you fill in the information for your own training instance.
The figure below shows the parts of a training instance website, and the names this guide uses for them.
FIG fig-alt=“Annotated example of a training instance website: the navigation bar with logos, the welcome section, the registration banner, the Next up section, the quick links, announcements, the team preview and the footer.”
In this chapter, you will learn how to:
How to add your training materials and instructor notes follows in the next chapter, Instance pages - Content.
Work on the branch of your training instance, for example release-2705, as described in Regular workflow.
Everything in this chapter happens in the data files in the data folder. Each data file explains how it works, in the lines starting with #: which fields are required, what they do, and the rules they must follow. Read these explanations carefully before you fill in a file.

title: 7  Instance pages - Data files
text:
7.1 Switch off template mode
Do this once, on the branch of your first training instance: the one you created from release-0000 (see Create your first new training instance). Later training instances start from this one, so these changes come along.

Replace the README
Your new branch still has the README of the template. Replace it with the ready-made README for a training instance, which is already on your branch, in the docs folder:

Open docs/_template-README.md, select all text, and copy it.
Open README.md, at the top level of your training instance repository. Select all text, and paste, so the copied text replaces it.
Delete the explanation at the top of the file, between <!-- and -->, and the note starting with > **Template:**.
Fill in the parts marked Write this yourself, and save the file.

The other parts of the README, between <!-- generated:... --> lines, fill in by themselves, from the data files of your training instance.






NoteOptional: delete docs/_template-README.md





You now no longer need docs/_template-README.md. In the Explorer panel, right-click the file and choose Delete.





Remove the template banner

Open data/website.yml.
Change template: true to template: false.
Save the file.

The yellow Want to use this template? banner disappears from the overview page.

title: 7  Instance pages - Data files
text:
7.2 Required information
Every training instance requires three data files to be filled in: course.yml, team.yml and website.yml.

The training: course.yml
data/course.yml describes this training instance. Most of it appears on the overview page and the Syllabus page.
Open data/course.yml, and work through it from the top down to the reuse part. The comments at the top list which fields are required and which are optional.
Leaving out optional fields. If an optional field doesn’t apply to your training, such as credits or examination:

delete it: the field name and all lines that belong to it; or

leave it empty: nothing after the colon, "" or [].







Tip



Use the same title, description, learning outcomes and keywords as on the landing page, unless this training instance is different. The landing page and the training instances then describe the same training.








NoteSelf-paced training






Leave out start_date and end_date.
Use duration for the expected workload, for example "About 10 hours".
Set mode and location to "Online".
Describe how participants work in instruction, for example "Self-study".










NoteTraining in cohorts





It depends on how you set up your training instances (see Training instances):

One training instance per cohort: fill in the dates of that cohort, as for any other training instance.
One training instance for several cohorts: leave out start_date and end_date, and list the cohorts and their dates on the Announcements or Practicalities page instead.




Reuse and citation. The reuse part at the bottom of data/course.yml describes how others may reuse and cite your training. Right now, the only thing to fill in is the licence:

licence and licence_url: CC BY 4.0 by default. Keep it, or change it. If you change it, also replace the text in LICENSE.md with the full text of your new licence.

Leave the other fields empty for now:

doi, version_doi, release_date and zenodo_communities belong to publishing your training instance on Zenodo, and are explained in FAIRification.
licence_id, version, website_url and preferred_citation can stay empty for most trainings. The template works out the version and the address of your website, and creates the citation from your team, title and DOI.







Important



Creating a training instance from one of your own earlier training instances? Then version_doi and release_date are probably filled in: empty them, because they belong to the earlier training instance. Keep doi: it stays the same for all your training instances.




The team: team.yml
The people in data/team.yml appear on the Team page, on the Syllabus page, and in a team preview on the overview page. They are also credited in the citation of the training instance.
Open data/team.yml and fill in each person. To add a person, copy a whole entry, from - given_names: to the line before the next person, paste it below, and change the values. To remove a person, delete their whole entry.






Important




Every person needs given_names, family_names, roles and affiliation. The roles are Training lead, Instructor and Contributor.
At least one person needs course_contact: true and an email: participants contact them with questions.



The overview page shows up to two people: training leads first, then instructors. Photos are optional: put them in the img/photos folder, and add their path under image.


The overview page: website.yml
data/website.yml sets the parts of the overview page that don’t come from other files. Open it, and work through the parts below. You can leave the rest of the file as it is: the content part follows in the next chapter, and the footer fills itself in.







Part of the file
What it sets




navbar → logos
The logos in the navigation bar. As on the landing page, the logo with primary: true (SciLifeLab) is always on the right, and you set the size of each logo with height. See Logos


welcome
The title, text and image of the welcome section. Put the image in the img folder


registration
The registration banner: when registration opens and closes, the link to the registration page or form, and the fee


pages
The texts on the quick links. You can usually leave them as they are: see the note below









NoteAbout the quick links





The overview page shows up to four quick links: cards that lead to the most important pages. Content and Syllabus always get one. The other pages, in the order Schedule, Practicalities, Preparation, Resources and FAQ, get one only when their data file contains information, while there’s room.
In the pages part of data/website.yml, you can change the title, description and icon of each quick link. The icons come from Bootstrap Icons.
To keep a page out of the quick links, delete its entry in data/website.yml. The page itself stays in the navigation bar, as long as its data file contains information.









NoteAbout the footer





You don’t need to change anything in the footer part of data/website.yml. The footer fills itself in:

The organisation (“By …”) comes from organizers in data/course.yml.
The licence (“Licensed under …”) comes from licence and licence_url under reuse in data/course.yml.
The GitHub logo links to your own repository, worked out automatically.

The built_with part credits the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template, which your website is built with. Please leave it as it is.









NoteAbout the content part





The content part at the bottom of data/website.yml lists the modules of your training materials, and the order in which they appear in the navigation. Leave it as it is for now: you’ll change it when you add your own materials, as described in Instance pages - Content.

title: 7  Instance pages - Data files
text:
7.3 Optional pages
The other data files are the flexible part of your training instance. Which ones you need depends on your training: a self-paced training has no schedule, an online training needs no practicalities about a venue, and a short workshop may not need announcements.








Page
Data file
Where it appears




Schedule
data/schedule.yml
Its own link in the navigation bar, and the Next up section on the overview page


Announcements
data/announcements.yml
The Information menu, and the two latest announcements on the overview page


Practicalities
data/practicalities.yml
The Information menu


Preparation
data/preparation.yml
The Information menu


FAQ
data/faq.yml
The Information menu


Resources
data/resources.yml
The Information menu



A page only appears when its data file contains information. Team and Syllabus are always in the Information menu: they come from the required files team.yml and course.yml.
Fill in the files you need, and leave out the others.

Fill in a page
Each data file starts with an explanation of its page. Read it carefully before you fill in the file: it describes what each field does, which fields are required, and how the page behaves. It also has a part called Leaving information out, which explains how to leave out one item or a whole section without breaking the page.






ImportantUsing a schedule? Read this first





The schedule needs a bit more care than the other pages, because the website uses its dates and times:

Each event, such as a lecture, an exercise or a break, is one entry, from - title: to content:. Every event needs a title, type, group, start and end.
Write dates and times exactly as explained in the file, for example 2027-05-12T09:00, and use one of the event types listed there.
Events with the same group, for example "Day 1", are shown together, in order of their start time.
To link an event to a page of your materials, fill in content with the path to that page, for example "content/module-1/introduction.qmd".

The Next up section on the overview page then always shows the next event, with a countdown, without you having to change anything during the training.





Leave a page out
Delete its data file, or delete everything in it. The page and its link in the navigation bar disappear by themselves.






Tip



Changed your mind later? Every data file is still in the template, on the release-0000 branch. Copy it from there, or from one of your earlier training instances.

title: 8  Instance pages - Content
text:
Before you start
The training materials are the heart of your training instance website: the pages participants work through. Unlike the rest of the website, these pages aren’t built from data files: you write them yourself, in Markdown, in .qmd files in the content folder. Your instructor notes, in the instructors folder, are also written in Markdown.
In this chapter, you will learn how to:
Everything in this chapter happens on the branch of your training instance, for example release-2705. Check the bottom-left corner of VS Code before you start: see Switch branch.

title: 8  Instance pages - Content
section: 8.1 Organise your training sections and pages
text:
8.1 Organise your training sections and pages

How the content folder is organised
Your training materials are in the content folder. It contains:

index.qmd: the Content introduction page, which introduces your materials and gives an overview of the sections.
_metadata.yml: the settings for all pages in the content folder, such as the table of contents on the right. You don’t need to change this file.
One folder for each section, with one .qmd file for each page in that section.

What a section is, is up to you: a module, a day, a topic or a week. You choose the names of the folders. The template’s examples use modules: module-1, module-2 and module-3.
On the website, each section gets its own dropdown menu in the navigation bar of the content pages, listing its pages.
For example, a training of three days, with a few topics per day:
content/
├── _metadata.yml      Settings for the content pages: leave as it is
├── index.qmd          The Content introduction page
├── day-1/             A section, with its pages:
│   ├── introduction.qmd
│   ├── topic-1.qmd
│   └── topic-2.qmd
├── day-2/
│   └── ...
└── day-3/
    └── ...






Tip



To see what ends up where, open the example folders in VS Code next to the preview in your browser, and compare the files with the website content pages.




Add a content section
Adding a section always takes two steps: create its folder inside the content folder, and list it in data/website.yml. A folder that isn’t listed doesn’t appear on the website.
Step 1: create the folder and its pages

In the Explorer panel in VS Code, right-click the content folder and choose New Folder….
Type the name of the folder, and press Enter. Use only lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens: no capital letters, no spaces. For example: day-1 or module-4.
Right-click your new folder and choose New File….
Type the name of the page, ending in .qmd, and press Enter. For example: introduction.qmd. Use lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens here too.
The new file opens. Type this header at the very top, with your own title:
---
title: "Introduction"
order: 1
---
Then write the text of the page below it, and save the file.
Add more pages to the folder the same way, with order: 2, order: 3 and so on.

The pages appear in the section’s dropdown menu in the order of their order numbers. To change the order, change the numbers.
Step 2: list the section in website.yml

Open data/website.yml, and scroll to the content part at the bottom. Each section has an entry of three lines, like this one from the template:
content:
  sections:
    - id: module-1
      label: "Module 1"
      title: "How to structure a page"
Copy a whole entry, from - id: to title:, and paste it below the last entry.
Change the three values to your new section:

id: the name of your folder, exactly as you typed it in step 1, for example day-1.
label: the short name in the navigation bar, for example "Day 1".
title: the text visitors see when they hover over the section in the navigation bar, for example "Getting started". Keep the spaces at the start of each line exactly as in the other entries!

Save the file, and check the preview: your section appears in the navigation bar of the content pages.







Important



The id must be exactly the same as the name of the folder, letter for letter. If you rename a folder later, also change its id, or the preview stops with an error that names the missing folder.


For example, after adding a section called day-1, the content part of data/website.yml looks like this:
content:
  sections:
    - id: module-1
      label: "Module 1"
      title: "How to structure a page"
    - id: day-1
      label: "Day 1"
      title: "Getting started"
The sections appear in the content navigation bar in the order of the section list in data/website.yml. To change the order, move whole entries up or down.


Remove a content section
Do two steps in this order, so the website never lists a folder that’s gone:

In data/website.yml, delete the section’s whole entry, from - id: to title:, and save the file.
In the Explorer panel, right-click the section’s folder in content and choose Delete. This deletes all its pages too.

title: 8  Instance pages - Content
text:
8.2 Images, presentations and other files






TipThe example pages are a guide



The example pages that come with the template are a short guide to writing training materials. They show how to write headings, lists, tables, callout boxes, images, videos and links, each with the Markdown to copy. Read them before you replace them with your own materials.


Put images, PDFs and other files you use on your pages in the docs folder. The example page Images, presentations and videos shows how to add them to a page.
You choose how to make and share your presentations. Common options:







Option
Good to know




Upload files to the repository, for example PDF slides
Archived with your training, so they stay available as long as the materials do. Keep files small: GitHub warns above 50 MB


Make presentations in Quarto
Part of your training website, and archived with it. Takes some getting used to


Link to an online tool, such as Google Slides
Easy to make and update together. The link can stop working, or need access rights that others don’t have



Whatever you choose, link to your materials from the module’s pages, so participants can find them, and note in the instructor notes where the editable versions are.

title: 8  Instance pages - Content
text:
8.3 Write instructor notes
The instructors folder holds notes for instructors: everything someone needs to teach this training, such as the timing of each module, how to prepare, and what to watch out for. The notes help your own team, and anyone who wants to reuse your training.

instructors/README.md covers the training as a whole: the timing, preparation and setup.
instructors/module-1.md, module-2.md and so on cover each module: its key points, teaching flow, exercises and common problems.

Fill in the example files, and add a file for each new module. The files are plain Markdown. On GitHub, instructors/README.md is shown as soon as you open the folder.






Warning



The instructor notes are not part of the website, but they are not private either: anyone can read them on GitHub, and they are archived on Zenodo with the materials. Never write anything that must stay secret, such as passwords, access codes, or answers to exams and graded assignments. Once pushed, deleting it does not remove it: it stays in the history of your repository.

title: 9  FAIRification
section: 9.2 Make your materials easy to cite
text:
9.2 Make your materials easy to cite
To make your training easier to cite, you can provide citation information in a CITATION.cff file. This file contains structured information about how your training materials should be cited, including the course title, authors, ORCID identifiers, licence, and links to the course repository and website.

9.2.1 Create the citation file for your course
The SciLifeLab Course Page Template already contains a CITATION.cff file in the root of the repository on the main branch. This file describes the template itself. When you use the template for your own course, replace the contents of CITATION.cff with citation information for your own training materials.

In the main branch, open CITATION.cff.
Delete the existing contents of the file.
Copy and paste the following starter text:

cff-version: 1.2.0
message: "If you use these training materials, please cite them as below."

title: "COURSE TITLE"

authors:
  - family-names: "SURNAME"
    given-names: "GIVEN NAME"
    orcid: "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"

license: CC-BY-4.0

repository-code: "https://github.com/ORGANISATION/REPOSITORY"
url: "https://ORGANISATION.github.io/REPOSITORY/"

references:
  - type: software
    title: "SciLifeLab Course Page Template"
    repository-code: "PERMANENT TEMPLATE REPOSITORY URL"

Replace the placeholder values with information about your course.








Field
What to enter




title
The title of your course or training materials.


family-names
The author’s family name or surname.


given-names
The author’s given name(s).


orcid
The author’s ORCID identifier, if they have one.


license
The licence under which the training materials are made available.


repository-code
The URL of the GitHub repository containing your course materials.


url
The URL of the published course website.









Important



Keep:
cff-version: 1.2.0
unchanged. This is the version of the Citation File Format specification, not the version of your course.




9.2.2 Add multiple authors
Add a separate entry under authors for each person who should be credited as an author of the training materials.
For example:
authors:
  - family-names: "Smith"
    given-names: "Anna"
    orcid: "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"

  - family-names: "Jones"
    given-names: "David"
    orcid: "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"
If an author does not have an ORCID, simply omit the orcid line:
authors:
  - family-names: "Jones"
    given-names: "David"






Tip



ORCID provides researchers with a persistent identifier that distinguishes them from other researchers. If your contributors have ORCID identifiers, include them in CITATION.cff.




9.2.3 Acknowledge this template in your course
The starter file contains the following entry:
references:
  - type: software
    title: "SciLifeLab Course Page Template"
    repository-code: "PERMANENT TEMPLATE REPOSITORY URL"
Keep this entry when adapting CITATION.cff for your course. It acknowledges the SciLifeLab Course Page Template as the resource used to create your course website.


9.2.4 Citation files for individual course instances
How you manage CITATION.cff depends on how you publish your course materials.
If your course is maintained as one continuously updated resource, you can maintain the citation information in the main branch.
If individual course instances are released separately (in this template by adding and publishing branches), their citation information may also differ. For example, different instances may have different contributors.
In this case, update CITATION.cff in the specific course-instance branch before creating the release. This allows the citation metadata for that release to reflect the people and materials associated with that particular course instance.






Tip



Before publishing a course instance, check that CITATION.cff contains the correct title, authors, ORCIDs, licence, repository URL, and course website URL for the materials you are releasing.



Quick reference
